blocks.text: The ability of water to dissolve a wide variety of substances is due to its two properties, the polarity of water molecules and the ability of water molecules to form hydrogen bonds.
The water molecule has distinct ends, each with a partial charge. Hydrogen atom is partially positive and oxygen atom is partially negative. Such molecules are called polar molecules.
Hydrogen bonds help in maintaining the three-dimensional structures of proteins and the double helix structure of DNA.

Partial negative charge at one end of a water molecule is attracted to partial positive of another water molecule. This weak attraction is called a hydrogen bond. Water forms a network of such bonds. Many of the properties of water are due to hydrogen bonds in water.
Without hydrogen bonding water would boil at – 80 °C and freeze at – 100 °C. making life impossible.

blocks.alt: A central water molecule (O with two H) surrounded by four water molecules. Dotted hydrogen bonds join each H of the central molecule to the O of a neighbour, and its O to an H of two other neighbours. O ends are marked (-) and H ends (+); one dotted bond is bracketed and labelled Hydrogen bond.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.6: Hydrogen bonds among water molecules (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.6).

blocks.text: Charged or polar molecules such as salts, sugars, amino acids dissolve readily in water and so are called hydrophilic ("water loving"). Uncharged or non-polar molecules such as lipids do not dissolve in water and are called hydrophobic ("water hating").

Due to the polar nature of water molecules, they gather around any other molecule that has an electrical charge, whether in the form of full charge (ions) or partial charge (polar molecules). For example, when sodium chloride (a salt) is placed in water, it breaks into positive (Na⁺) and negative ions (Cl⁻). These ions are surrounded by opposite polar ends of water molecules (Figure 4.7).

blocks.alt: Left: a NaCl crystal, a packed lattice of large blue Cl- and small red Na+ ions. An arrow leads to dissolved ions: two red Na+ ions, each ringed by water molecules with their O ends towards it, and two blue Cl- ions, each ringed by water molecules with an H end towards it. Water molecules are pink with yellow-green H. Labels: NaCl, Na+, Cl-.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.7: Water as a solvent of inorganic molecules (NaCl) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.7).

blocks.text: Similarly, when a glucose is placed in water, the molecules of water form hydrogen bonds with polar hydroxyl groups of glucose molecules. In this way, glucose dissolves in water (Figure 4.8). It means that charged or polar molecules are soluble in water. In the state of solution, ions and molecules can react with each other easily. So, water provides a medium for chemical reactions i.e., metabolism of cells.

blocks.alt: A dark brown glucose molecule labelled Glucose sits on a glowing yellow hexagon; its edge is studded with pink hydroxyl groups, each with a small green H. Five water molecules (a large pink O with two green H) around it are joined to hydroxyl groups by dotted hydrogen bonds. Labels: Hydrogen bond (top), Water (right), Hydroxyl group (left).
blocks.caption: Figure 4.8: Water as a solvent of organic molecules (glucose) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.8).

blocks.text: So, charged or polar molecules are soluble in water. In the state of solution, ions and molecules can react with each other easily. So, water provides a medium for metabolism (chemical reactions in cells).

Polar molecules such as salts, sugars, and amino acids dissolve readily in water and are called hydrophilic (water-loving). Uncharged or non-polar molecules such as lipids do not dissolve in water and are called hydrophobic (water-hating).
